passage:
Dear Chandrika,
I've started this letter three times, so I'll just say it. I'm sorry for the way I've treated you since you joined as the new girl on the scholarship.
When you wore old sports shoes to the inter-house race, I was the one who called them 'government issue'. I rolled my eyes when you asked the teacher to repeat things. I think I believed kids like you were lucky to be here and kids like me deserved to be.
Then we were paired for the chemistry project, and you understood titration in ten minutes while I needed a week. You told me you tutor your brother every evening after helping at your mother's tailoring shop. I go home to a cook and a private tutor.
I keep thinking about how much of what I called 'me' was just what I was handed.
You didn't deserve any of it. If you'd like, I'd really like to be friends.
Karthik

qa.q: What did Karthik call Chandrika's sports shoes?
qa.a: 'Government issue'.

qa.q: What is Karthik feeling while writing the letter?
qa.a: Karthik feels ashamed and regretful, having started the letter three times before managing to say sorry.

qa.q: What would you advise Karthik to do next, beyond the letter?
qa.a: Treat Chandrika as an equal day to day, and speak up when others mock scholarship students.

qa.q: How might Chandrika have felt when her shoes were mocked?
qa.a: She probably felt humiliated and unwelcome, judged for money rather than for who she is.

grounding: A letter from a teen who looked down on a scholarship classmate, noticing how privilege shaped them and choosing to treat her by who she is.

passage: Honestly? At fourteen I was a snob, and I didn't even know it. I'm Usha, by the way, and this is the part of school I'm least proud of. There was a girl in my class, Simran, who came on the fee-waiver scheme. She carried her lunch in a steel dabba with a dent, and I'd make little comments to my friends: 'Smells like the bus stop.' I thought I was funny. Then in Class 9 we both got picked for the quiz team, and we practised at her place once. Tiny room, her mother stitching blouses by the window, Simran answering every capital city while stirring dal. I sat on that floor thinking, everything I have, I was handed. She built hers. After that I stopped the comments and started asking her things, like how she remembered so much. We won the district round together. She still teases me about the dabba jokes, and she's right to.

qa.q: What did Simran carry her lunch in?
qa.a: A steel dabba with a dent.

qa.q: What was Usha feeling while sitting on the floor of Simran's room?
qa.a: Usha felt humbled and ashamed, seeing that everything Usha had was handed over while Simran built hers.

qa.q: What changed in how Usha treated Simran after the visit?
qa.a: Usha stopped the comments and started asking Simran real questions, treating her by who she is.

qa.q: How might Simran have seen Usha's comments at the time?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and looked down on, which is why she still teases Usha about them now.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen who sneered at a poorer classmate, then noticed their own privilege and began treating her by who she is.

passage: Vaibhav had always told the group he lived 'near the mall'. In truth, his family's one-room home was behind it, above his father's ironing stall, where Papa pressed clothes for the whole lane from seven in the morning. On Sunday, Siddharth turned up unannounced to return a charger. Vaibhav saw him from the stall and wanted the ground to swallow him. His stomach twisted; he almost pretended not to know Papa. 'Uncle, this is the fastest ironing I've ever seen,' Siddharth said, watching Papa fold a shirt in three sharp moves. Papa laughed and pressed Siddharth's crumpled collar for free. Upstairs, Siddharth ate two parathas and asked if Vaibhav could teach him to fold like that. Later, alone, Vaibhav thought about the kids at school who had taught him to feel small. Papa's hands had paid for his school, his books, even that charger.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav's father do?
qa.a: He runs an ironing stall, pressing clothes for the whole lane from seven in the morning.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling when he saw Siddharth from the stall?
qa.a: He felt deeply ashamed and panicked, his stomach twisting, wanting the ground to swallow him.

qa.q: What could Vaibhav do differently next time friends visit?
qa.a: Give his real address and introduce Papa with pride, trusting that friends like Siddharth care about him, not the house.

qa.q: How does Siddharth see Vaibhav's home and Papa's work?
qa.a: He sees skill and warmth, admiring Papa's fast ironing and enjoying the parathas 😊

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed of his father's work and home when a friend visits, and the friend's respect showing that dignity of work is real.

passage:
'Amma, why did you come to the gate in your uniform?' Keerthana hissed, pulling her aside.
'I came straight from the hospital, kanna. My shift ended late.'
Ishita walked up, smiling. 'Hi Aunty! Are you a nurse?'
Keerthana froze.
'No, ma. I clean the wards,' Amma said simply.
'Oh, my Paati was in that hospital last year,' Ishita said. 'The cleaning staff were the only ones who talked to her at night. She still talks about one aunty who brought her an extra blanket.'
Amma smiled. 'Night shift is lonely for patients.'
On the walk home, Keerthana was quiet. 'I wrote "business" on the form for your job, Amma.'
'I know. I saw the form.'
'I'm sorry. I was scared they'd laugh.'
'Did Ishita laugh?'
'No. She said thank you.'
Amma squeezed her daughter's hand. 'Clean wards save lives too, kanna. Write it properly tomorrow.'

qa.q: What does Amma do at the hospital?
qa.a: She cleans the wards.

qa.q: Why did Keerthana freeze when Ishita asked if Amma was a nurse?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and scared that her friend would laugh at her mother's job.

qa.q: What should Keerthana do with the form tomorrow, and why?
qa.a: Write Amma's real job, because the work has dignity and a true friend like Ishita respects it.

qa.q: How does Ishita see the cleaning staff at the hospital?
qa.a: With gratitude, remembering how they talked to her Paati at night and brought an extra blanket.

grounding: Shows a teen ashamed of her mother's cleaning job who sees, through a friend's respect, that the shame is learned and the work has dignity.

passage: Through the thin wall of their Pune flat, Jahnavi heard it again past midnight: Papa's voice low and tight, Mumma crying. 'The loan instalment and her coaching fees in the same month, how?' Jahnavi lay rigid. The coaching was her idea. Her new calculator. Her bus pass. By morning she had decided to quit coaching without telling anyone. At breakfast her little brother Vishal chattered about a cricket bat, and Jahnavi's throat closed. After he left for school, she said, 'I heard you last night. Is it because of my fees?' Mumma put down the dosa ladle. 'It's not your fault, bachcha. We had a loss at the shop. We're sorting it.' 'Can I help? I could stop coaching.' Papa shook his head. 'Your job is studying. You help by telling us when you're worried, and by switching off the geyser. The rest is ours.' Jahnavi felt the knot loosen, just a little.

qa.q: What did Mumma say caused the money trouble?
qa.a: A loss at the shop.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling as she lay awake listening?
qa.a: She felt scared and guilty, believing her coaching and bus pass were costing the family too much.

qa.q: What did Jahnavi do well the next morning?
qa.a: She asked her parents directly instead of quitting in secret, and offered help within her role.

qa.q: How do Jahnavi's parents see her offer to stop coaching?
qa.a: They see it as loving but not her job; they want her to study and leave the fixing to them.

grounding: Shows a teen who overhears her parents fight over a loan and fees, feels scared and guilty, asks what is happening and is reminded she is not the fixer.

passage:
'Jeevan, the school sent another reminder,' Mummy whispered in the kitchen. 'The third one. And the landlord...'
'I know, Lata. I know.' Papa's voice cracked.
Himani stood in the corridor with the fee slip in her bag, the one she hadn't given them yet. She walked in.
'Papa, is it about my fees?'
They both turned. Mummy wiped her hands. 'You heard.'
'Some. I'm sorry I cost so much.'
Papa sat down heavily. 'Beta, you don't cost. You're our daughter. My hours at the mill were cut, that's all.'
'Then I'll ask about the fee waiver. Sharma Ma'am said there's a form for families going through a hard time.'
Papa hesitated, then nodded. 'That would help. Bring the form and we'll fill it together.'
'And I'll stop asking for new stuff.'
Mummy pulled her close. 'Just keep telling us what you hear, okay? Don't carry it alone. The worrying is our job.'

qa.q: Why was Papa earning less?
qa.a: His hours at the mill were cut.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling as she stood in the corridor with the fee slip?
qa.a: She felt scared and guilty, thinking her fees were the reason for her parents' worry.

qa.q: Which of Himani's offers fits her role, and why?
qa.a: Asking Sharma Ma'am about the fee waiver form, because it's a small, age-appropriate step while her parents handle the rest.

qa.q: How does Papa see Himani's apology for costing so much?
qa.a: It clearly pains him; he insists she doesn't cost anything, she's their daughter.

grounding: Shows a teen who overhears her parents' worry about fees, feels guilty, asks what is happening and helps within her role while her parents carry the rest.

passage:
Dear Amma,
I'm leaving this on your sewing machine because I know you'll find it before anyone else.
I've noticed things. You've stopped buying fruit, you say you're 'not hungry' at dinner, and when the phone rings you take it outside. Rajni Aunty mentioned you've been taking stitching orders late at night. You tell me everything is fine, and I know you say it so I won't worry.
But Amma, I worry more when I have to guess. I can handle the truth, even if it's hard.
Also, I don't need new cricket spikes for the trials. Rajni Aunty's son has an old pair that fits me. And I can skip the school trip to Mysore this year. I'm not saying this to make you feel bad. You and Appa have always given me more than enough.
Can we talk on Sunday, just us? Whatever it is, I'd rather know.
Your son,
Naveen

qa.q: Where is Naveen leaving the letter?
qa.a: On Amma's sewing machine.

qa.q: Why does Naveen worry more when Amma says everything is fine?
qa.a: He feels anxious having to guess, and he senses the trouble anyway from the missing fruit and calls taken outside 😔

qa.q: What makes Naveen's letter a kind way to raise the problem?
qa.a: He says he can handle honesty, adjusts his own asks, and makes clear he isn't blaming his parents.

qa.q: How might Amma feel reading the letter?
qa.a: She might feel touched and a little exposed, proud of her son yet sad he noticed what she tried to hide.

grounding: A letter from a teen who senses his mother hiding money trouble, asking kindly for honesty and adjusting his asks without blame.

passage: You know what, Neelam, I'll tell you why I was so weird all last month. I'm Keerthana, your best friend, so I'm allowed one weird month a year. Appa kept leaving at nine in his office shirt, same as always. But one afternoon I saw him on the bench at the bus depot at two o'clock, just sitting. And he'd stopped asking about my dance fees, which he never forgets. I knew something was wrong, but he kept smiling at dinner like a TV dad. I was angry at first, honestly. Why lie? Then I thought, it's pride, and it's because he loves me. So one night I made him tea and said, 'Appa, I saw you at the depot. You don't have to act for me. I'm old enough.' He went quiet, then told me his company had shut. I said I'd pause dance till things settle, and he cried a bit. Now we talk. It's better.

qa.q: Where did Keerthana see Appa at two o'clock?
qa.a: On the bench at the bus depot, just sitting.

qa.q: What was Keerthana feeling at first about Appa hiding it?
qa.a: Keerthana felt angry and hurt at first, wondering why Appa would lie.

qa.q: What did Keerthana say that helped Appa open up?
qa.a: Over tea, Keerthana gently said Appa didn't have to act, and offered to pause dance without blaming him.

qa.q: Why might Appa have kept leaving in his office shirt?
qa.a: Out of pride and love, wanting to protect his child from worry about the company shutting.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen who senses a father hiding job loss, tells him kindly they can handle honesty, and adjusts their asks without blame.

passage: The deadline for the Goa trip money was nine the next morning, and Rajni's family couldn't pay it. That evening the class group was a flood of packing photos, new phones and 'Can't wait!!' messages. Rajni's old phone froze twice just loading them. Something sour rose in her chest. Why do they get everything? Then Joseph texted: 'Just borrow it from me, pay me back whenever.' Her thumb hovered. She could also say she was 'busy that week'. Nobody would know. Rajni put the phone down and went up to the terrace. 'Okay,' she told herself. 'I'm jealous. That's real.' She thought about what she did have: Nani's stories, her place on the school kabaddi team, Saturday cycling with her brother. She replied to Joseph: 'Thanks, really. But I don't want to owe you. I'm not going this time. Send me beach photos.'

qa.q: What did Joseph offer Rajni?
qa.a: To lend her the money, paid back whenever.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling as the packing photos flooded in?
qa.a: She felt bitter and jealous, something sour rising in her chest.

qa.q: What went right in how Rajni handled it?
qa.a: She named her envy honestly, thought about what she has, and turned down both borrowing and pretending.

qa.q: How might Joseph see Rajni's reply?
qa.a: He may be a little disappointed but respect her honesty, since she thanked him warmly and asked for photos.

grounding: Shows a teen envious of friends' trip and phones who acknowledges the bitterness, focuses on what she has and refuses to borrow or pretend.

passage: At Vishal's birthday lunch in a Bandra café, every phone on the table was new except Madhuri's, the cracked one with sticky tape on the back. When Vishal passed his round, showing off the camera, Madhuri laughed along, but inside she felt small and bitter. Last month Papa had said, gently, no new phone this year. Under the table she almost typed a lie into the group: 'mine's just a backup, my real one is being fixed.' She deleted it. Sipping her lime soda, she let herself admit it: I'm envious, and that's allowed. She thought of what her old phone held: two years of voice notes from Aaji, her whole drawing folder. When Vishal asked her to take the group photo, she said, 'Use yours, my camera's rubbish,' and grinned. Nobody cared. They were too busy fighting over the last brownie.

qa.q: What was on the back of Madhuri's phone?
qa.a: Sticky tape, on the cracked phone.

qa.q: What was Madhuri feeling when Vishal passed his phone round?
qa.a: She felt small and bitter, envious of everyone's new phones while laughing along.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Madhuri, and why?
qa.a: Deleting the lie and admitting her envy to herself, so she didn't have to keep up a pretence 🙂

qa.q: How does Vishal seem to see Madhuri's old phone?
qa.a: He doesn't seem to care at all; he just wants a group photo and a share of the brownie.

grounding: Shows a teen bitter about friends' new phones who acknowledges the envy, values what she has and avoids pretending to keep up.

passage:
'Ma'am, I'm thinking of leaving after Class 10,' Jaya said, standing by the staffroom door.
Preeti Ma'am looked up from the copies. 'Leaving? You're my best in biology. Sit. What's happening?'
'Papa's auto broke down, and the repairs... Amma's doing extra cooking orders. My cousin says the garment unit takes girls like me.'
'Have you talked to your parents about this?'
'Not yet. I didn't want them to feel bad.'
'Talk to them tonight. And listen. There's a state merit scholarship for Class 11 and 12. You're eligible. I'll help you apply.'
'But that doesn't help right now.'
'True. What about tutoring the Class 6 kids in your lane, two evenings a week? Safe, near home, and your studies stay first.'
Jaya hesitated. 'I could do that.'
'Bring your parents on Saturday. We'll plan together. Nobody's dropping out of my biology class.'

qa.q: What scholarship did Preeti Ma'am mention?
qa.a: A state merit scholarship for Class 11 and 12.

qa.q: Why hadn't Jaya talked to her parents yet?
qa.a: She felt worried and protective, not wanting them to feel bad about the money trouble.

qa.q: What plan did Preeti Ma'am suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Apply for the scholarship, tutor younger kids near home, and meet with her parents, keeping education first.

qa.q: How does Preeti Ma'am see Jaya's idea of leaving?
qa.a: She sees it as losing a bright student and a problem to plan around together, not a done deal.

grounding: Shows a teen considering dropping out to help her family who talks to a teacher and plans a scholarship and safe tutoring with education first.

passage: Last year, the month after Dad's shop flooded, I seriously thought about quitting school. I'm Abhinav, and I was sure I'd be more use earning. Farhan's uncle had a phone repair counter in the market and said I could work there full-time. I didn't tell anyone. I just started skipping the last two periods to sit at the counter. Then our class teacher, Mr Dsouza, rang home about the missed classes, and it all came out at dinner. Mum cried, which was worse than shouting. But then we actually talked, all of us. Mr Dsouza helped me find a scholarship for the board year, and Farhan's uncle agreed I could work Sunday mornings only, at the counter where he could keep an eye on me. I still help. But I'm in school, and Dad says that's the help he wanted most.

qa.q: What did Farhan's uncle offer Abhinav?
qa.a: Full-time work at his phone repair counter in the market.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when Mum cried at dinner?
qa.a: Abhinav felt guilty and shaken, finding her tears worse than shouting.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Abhinav skipped classes in secret; talking openly with family and the teacher led to a scholarship and safe Sunday-only work.

qa.q: How does Dad see the help Abhinav gives?
qa.a: He values Abhinav staying in school as the help he wanted most.

grounding: A first-person account of a teen who nearly dropped out to earn, then talked with family and a teacher and found a scholarship and safe part-time work.

passage: On the first day of Class 10 at the Jaipur municipal school, Chinmay grabbed Jagdish's physics book and read out the name on the inside cover. 'Property of Mahesh Kumar! Bhai, even your books are second-hand?' Some boys laughed. Jagdish's shirt, faded from three years of washing, suddenly felt see-through. His ears burned. But he held out his hand. 'My cousin's. Same chapters as yours. Can I have it back?' Chinmay tossed it on the desk, a little thrown by the calm. The comments kept coming that week, though: 'Hand-me-down Jagdish.' On Friday Jagdish told Mrs Saxena, the class teacher. She called Chinmay aside at once and phoned his parents that evening. Walking home, Jagdish opened the physics book. Mahesh bhaiya had underlined every important line in red. Honestly, that was better than new.

qa.q: Whose name was written inside Jagdish's physics book?
qa.a: Mahesh Kumar's, his cousin's.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling when the boys laughed?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and exposed, as if his faded shirt were see-through, his ears burning.

qa.q: Which of Jagdish's responses worked, and why?
qa.a: Replying calmly and then telling the teacher when it kept going, because both stopped the teasing without a fight.

qa.q: How might Chinmay have felt when Jagdish stayed calm?
qa.a: He was a little thrown, since he expected embarrassment, not a steady request for the book.

grounding: Shows a teen teased about second-hand books and uniform who replies calmly and tells a teacher when it persists, keeping his dignity.

passage:
'Oye, Irfan, nice shoes. Did the tape come free with them?' Amandeep called across the corridor.
A couple of boys sniggered. Irfan looked down at the black tape on his left sole.
'It holds fine,' he said evenly. 'Keeps the rain out.'
'Tell your dad to buy you real ones.'
'My Abbu's working double shifts. The shoes are fine.'
Amandeep grinned. 'Sure, sure.'
Irfan kept walking. His friend Neil caught up. 'You were so calm. I'd have punched him.'
'I wanted to,' Irfan admitted. 'My face was hot. But then he'd get to be the victim.'
'He did this yesterday too, with your bag.'
'And last week with my jacket.' Irfan stopped outside the staffroom. 'Three times is enough. I'm telling Gill sir.'
Five minutes later Gill sir walked into class, asked Amandeep to step out, and spoke to him quietly in the corridor. Nobody mentioned Irfan's shoes after that.

qa.q: What was on Irfan's left sole?
qa.a: Black tape.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel when Amandeep mocked his shoes?
qa.a: He felt angry and embarrassed, his face hot, even though he answered calmly.

qa.q: Why was telling Gill sir the right step?
qa.a: The teasing was persistent, three times now, so a teacher needed to step in.

qa.q: How does Neil see Irfan's calm reply?
qa.a: He's impressed, since he would have punched Amandeep, and he backs Irfan by pointing out the pattern 👍

grounding: Shows a teen teased about taped shoes who replies calmly with dignity and tells a teacher when the teasing persists.

passage: During the cricket season, every video Bhupen watched in his village near Jorhat came with the same ad: a smiling man waving notes, 'Predict the match, win big, start with just a little!' The tea garden had cut his family's wages, and the ad felt like it was talking straight to him. Then a stranger in a local cricket fans' group messaged: 'Send a small amount to my number, I'll double it by tonight. Many boys from your area are earning.' Bhupen's thumb hovered. At the tea stall, his friend Yogesh saw the message and went pale. 'Don't. My cousin sent his whole savings to a man like this. Gone.' That evening Bhupen showed the chat to his uncle, the village schoolteacher. His uncle read it slowly. 'Anyone who promises to double your money is taking it, not giving it.' Together they blocked the number and reported it.

qa.q: What did the stranger promise to do with Bhupen's money?
qa.a: Double it by tonight.

qa.q: Why did the ad feel like it was talking straight to Bhupen?
qa.a: He felt worried about his family's cut wages and tempted by the hope of quick money.

qa.q: What did Bhupen do that kept him safe?
qa.a: He didn't send anything, showed the chat to his uncle, and they blocked and reported the number together.

qa.q: How does Yogesh see the stranger's message?
qa.a: He sees it as the same trap that took his cousin's savings, so he warns Bhupen at once.

grounding: Shows a teen targeted by a betting and money-doubling offer who recognises the hook, asks an adult and never sends money.

passage:
Dear Maa,
I didn't want to say this in front of everyone at Diwali, so I'm writing instead.
I'm really grateful to Vasudha Mausi for paying my school fees these two years. I know we couldn't have managed. I'm going to thank her properly, and one day I want to do the same for someone.
But Maa, every time we visit, she mentions it. 'Study hard, I'm paying, remember.' At Diwali she said it in front of all the cousins, and I wanted to disappear. I felt thankful and small at the same time, and I hate feeling both.
I'm not asking you to fight with her. Could you, gently, tell her how it feels for us? Maybe that we know, we'll never forget, and she doesn't need to remind us?
I'll write her a thank-you card this week. I just need your help with the rest.
Love,
Abhinav

qa.q: What does Vasudha Mausi say on every visit?
qa.a: 'Study hard, I'm paying, remember.'

qa.q: What does Abhinav feel when Mausi mentions the fees?
qa.a: Abhinav feels grateful and humiliated at once, wanting to disappear when it's said in front of the cousins.

qa.q: What makes Abhinav's plan a balanced one?
qa.a: Abhinav will thank Mausi sincerely with a card and asks Maa to set a gentle boundary, instead of fighting.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Mausi see her reminders?
qa.a: She may think she's motivating Abhinav, not realising the reminders feel humiliating.

grounding: A letter from a teen grateful yet humiliated by a relative who pays fees and keeps mentioning it, planning to thank her and asking a parent to set a boundary.

passage: Chinmay, you asked why I went so quiet at Jethu's place last Sunday. I'll tell you, since you're the only one who won't make it a joke. I'm Arnab, the lucky nephew, remember? Jethu pays my hostel fees. At every family lunch he says it: 'Arnab, this fish is from my pocket too, eh?' Everyone laughs. I laugh. And inside I feel two things at once: thankful, because without him I'd be out of school, and humiliated, because Baba stares at his plate every time. So this week I did two things. I wrote Jethu a proper thank-you letter and told him I'll pay it forward to some kid someday. And I asked Baba, gently, if he could ask Jethu to stop saying it at lunch. Baba went red, then said he'd been wanting to for months. He talked to Jethu yesterday. Fingers crossed for next Sunday.

qa.q: What does Jethu say at every family lunch?
qa.a: 'Arnab, this fish is from my pocket too, eh?'

qa.q: What two feelings does Arnab describe?
qa.a: He feels thankful that Jethu keeps him in school and humiliated when it's joked about at lunch.

qa.q: Which two steps did Arnab take, and why are they wise?
qa.a: He wrote Jethu a sincere thank-you and asked Baba to set a gentle boundary, keeping both gratitude and dignity.

qa.q: How does Baba seem to feel at those lunches?
qa.a: He seems ashamed, staring at his plate, and relieved when Arnab gives him a reason to speak to Jethu.

grounding: A spoken account of a teen grateful yet humiliated by an uncle paying fees and reminding them, thanking him and asking a parent to set a boundary.

passage: The summer our electricity got cut for two weeks, I did my Class 10 revision under the streetlight outside our building. I'm Himani, and that's the summer I got angry in a useful way. I was also angry in a useless way, for a while. I'd watch Papa come home tired from the loading dock and think, why couldn't you have done better? Then I'd feel disgusted with myself for thinking it. My friend Farhan, whose family runs the tea stall on our corner, sat with me under the light one night and said, 'You know your papa carries sacks all day so you can sit here with books, right?' That stayed with me. I stopped blaming Papa, and I stopped blaming myself for our small flat. I kept the anger, but I pointed it at the syllabus. I topped the district. Papa framed the certificate above the gas stove.

qa.q: Where did Himani revise when the electricity was cut?
qa.a: Under the streetlight outside the building.

qa.q: What was Himani feeling when watching Papa come home tired?
qa.a: Himani felt resentful, then guilty and disgusted at having such a thought about Papa.

qa.q: How did Himani use the anger in a helpful way?
qa.a: By pointing it at the syllabus instead of at Papa or at being poor, which led to topping the district.

qa.q: How does Farhan see Papa's work?
qa.a: Farhan sees it as a sacrifice made so Himani can study, and wants Himani to see it that way too.

grounding: A first-person account of money stress fuelling a teen's drive, while the narrator learns not to blame family or self for being poor.

passage: Counsellor's note, Thursday. Ankita (Class 12) came in after the mock results. She had topped physics, but she was shaking. 'I'm doing this so I never have to live like we do,' she said. 'Sometimes I hate our house. I hate that Amma sews till midnight. And I hate myself for being ashamed of her.' She told me her brother Harish left school at sixteen to drive an auto and pays for her tuition. I told her the drive was real and hers to use, and that being poor is not a failing in her or her family. We talked about what she's proud of at home: Harish's jokes, Amma's embroidery that wins at the fair every year. She left saying she'd aim for the engineering entrance for herself and for them, not against them. I've booked a follow-up in two weeks and shared scholarship lists with her class teacher.

qa.q: Who pays for Ankita's tuition?
qa.a: Her brother Harish, who left school at sixteen to drive an auto.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling when she came in after the mock results?
qa.a: She was shaking, driven but also full of shame and anger at her home and at herself.

qa.q: How did the counsellor help Ankita use her drive?
qa.a: The counsellor affirmed the drive, said being poor isn't a failing, and helped her name what she's proud of at home.

qa.q: How might Harish see Ankita's result in physics?
qa.a: He would likely feel proud, since the tuition he pays for is helping her aim high 🙂

grounding: A counsellor's note on a teen whose money stress fuels her ambition, helped not to hate her family or herself for being poor.
